title: A date, a tagline and a tour bus
lede: Sega of America had little money and seven months. It built the launch around a date people could remember and a campaign that explained almost nothing.

blocks.title: “It’s thinking”
blocks.body:
Moore’s brief was to “somewhat apologize for the past” while recalling what people liked about Sega in the Genesis years. The answer was a run of 15-second spots that never quite said what the machine was. “It was mysterious,” he said. “First of all, if you didn’t know, maybe we didn’t want to talk to you.”[^7]

The launch itself was staged as an event: 9/9/99 for $199, a spot on the MTV Video Music Awards, and sponsorship of rock tours.[^6] A second series, “In the Box,” put NFL and NBA players alongside characters from the games.[^7]

blocks.text: We were a big brand. But then it all went pear-shaped in Christmas 2000.

blocks.title: The feature the ads undersold
blocks.caption: Original illustration.
blocks.body: Every console shipped with a modem, and by March 2000 Sega counted 1.12 million registered network users: 550,000 in Japan, 330,000 in the United States and 240,000 in Europe.[^1] Sega’s own U.S. online service, SegaNet, opened a year after launch.[^14]

blocks.title: The price, cut by cut
rows: With a $150 rebate for an 18-month SegaNet contract[^15]
To clear about 2 million unsold consoles[^5][^4]
blocks.source: In Japan the price fell from ¥29,800 at launch to ¥19,900.[^4]
